g10-physics-up2-t1.overview: To describe motion, we first need to talk about where something is (position) and how far it has moved from where it started (displacement). These ideas are the foundation of kinematics.
objectives: Define position relative to a reference point
Distinguish between distance and displacement
Use a number line or coordinate system to describe position
Understand that displacement is a vector while distance is a scalar
g10-physics-up2-t1.simple: Position is WHERE something is — like 'the car is at the 5 km mark'. Distance is HOW FAR you traveled altogether — like 'we drove 100 km'. Displacement is how far you are from where you started, in a straight line — like 'we ended up 20 km north of home'. Even if you drive around in circles for hours, if you end where you started, your displacement is zero!
g10-physics-up2-t1.detailed:
Position is the location of an object relative to a chosen reference point (origin). On a number line, position can be positive or negative depending on which side of the origin the object is.

Distance (d) is the total length of the path traveled. It is a scalar — always positive, never decreases, and doesn't tell you direction.

Displacement (Δs or Δx) is the change in position: the straight-line distance from the starting point to the ending point, with direction. It is a vector.

Displacement = final position − initial position: Δx = x₂ − x₁

If an object moves from position 2 m to position 10 m, its displacement is 8 m in the positive direction. If it then returns to 2 m, the total distance is 16 m but the total displacement is 0 m.

keyTerms.def: The location of an object relative to a reference point (origin).
Total path length traveled; a scalar quantity.
Change in position (final − initial); a vector quantity.
The zero mark from which positions are measured.
Greek letter meaning 'change in' a quantity.

formulas.name: Displacement
formulas.meaning: Displacement equals final position minus initial position.
formulas.when: To find how far (and in which direction) an object moved between two positions.
formulas.example: An object moves from x₁ = 2 m to x₂ = 10 m. Δx = 10 − 2 = 8 m.

workedExamples.problem: A student walks from the classroom (position 0 m) to the library (position 50 m east), then to the cafeteria (position 20 m east). Find the total distance and the displacement.
workedExamples.given: Start: 0 m. Library: +50 m. Cafeteria: +20 m.
workedExamples.formula: Distance = total path. Displacement = final − initial.
workedExamples.calculation: The displacement is +20 m (east of start).

commonMistakes: Using distance and displacement interchangeably. Distance is the path; displacement is the straight-line change in position.
Forgetting that displacement can be negative (direction matters!).
Forgetting to state the direction of a displacement.
applications: Satellite navigation systems calculate displacement, not distance, to give you the shortest route.
Physiotherapists track displacement during joint rehabilitation exercises.
Sports science measures a runner's displacement (not just distance) to analyze efficiency.
g10-physics-up2-t1.summary: Position is where an object is. Distance is the total path traveled (scalar). Displacement = final position − initial position (vector). You can travel far but have zero displacement if you return to the start.

questions.q: Which quantity tells you the total length of the path traveled?
questions.explanation: Distance is the total path length — a scalar. Displacement is the straight-line change in position.

questions.q: An object moves from position −3 m to position 5 m. Its displacement is:
questions.explanation: Δx = 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8 m, in the positive direction.

questions.q: A person who runs around a 400 m track once has a displacement of 400 m.
questions.explanation: They end where they started, so displacement = 0 m. The distance was 400 m.

questions.q: What is the displacement of an object that returns exactly to its starting point?
questions.explanation: Final position = initial position, so Δx = 0.

questions.q: A delivery truck drives 10 km east, then 10 km west, back to the depot. Compare distance and displacement.
questions.explanation: Distance = 10 + 10 = 20 km. Displacement = 0 because it returns to the start.

questions.q: A car moves from position 15 m to position 42 m. Find its displacement.

g10-physics-up2-t2.overview: Velocity describes how fast an object's position changes AND in what direction. Average velocity considers the whole trip; instantaneous velocity tells you the velocity at a specific instant.
objectives: Define average velocity and calculate it from displacement and time
Distinguish between speed and velocity
Explain instantaneous velocity
Interpret velocity values and signs
g10-physics-up2-t2.simple: Speed is 'how fast' — like 60 km/h. Velocity is 'how fast AND which way' — like 60 km/h north. Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. If you drive a windy road for 2 hours and end up only 40 km from home, your average velocity is 20 km/h in the direction of home — even if your speedometer showed 80 km/h the whole time!
g10-physics-up2-t2.detailed:
Speed is the rate of change of distance: speed = distance ÷ time. It's a scalar.

Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: velocity = displacement ÷ time. It's a vector — it has direction.

Average velocity: vavg = Δx / Δt = (x₂ − x₁) / (t₂ − t₁)

Average velocity depends only on the total displacement and total time — not on the details of the path.

Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a single moment. On a position–time graph, it's the slope of the tangent line at that point. Your car's speedometer shows instantaneous speed.

The sign of velocity tells direction: positive means moving in the positive direction, negative means moving opposite. In SI units, velocity is measured in meters per second (m/s).

keyTerms.def: Rate of change of distance; scalar (m/s).
Rate of change of displacement; vector (m/s).
Total displacement divided by total time.
Velocity at a specific instant; slope of tangent on x–t graph.
Motion at constant velocity (no acceleration).

formulas.name: Average velocity
formulas.meaning: Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time interval.
formulas.when: To find average velocity over a trip given total displacement and time.

workedExamples.problem: A cyclist travels 360 m east in 45 s, then 240 m west in 35 s. Find (a) average speed and (b) average velocity.
workedExamples.given: East: 360 m in 45 s. West: 240 m in 35 s.
workedExamples.formula: speed = total distance / total time; velocity = displacement / total time
workedExamples.substitution: Total distance = 360 + 240 = 600 m. Total time = 45 + 35 = 80 s. Speed = 600/80 = 7.5 m/s.
workedExamples.calculation: Displacement = 360 − 240 = 120 m east. Velocity = 120/80 = 1.5 m/s east.
workedExamples.answer: Average speed = 7.5 m/s, average velocity = 1.5 m/s east

commonMistakes: Confusing speed and velocity: speed has no direction, velocity does.
Using distance instead of displacement for velocity.
Forgetting to state the direction of velocity.
applications: Traffic enforcement: average speed cameras measure average velocity over a stretch.
Sports analytics: average sprint velocity vs. top (instantaneous) speed.
Aviation: ground velocity combines airspeed with wind — a vector sum.
g10-physics-up2-t2.summary: Speed = distance/time (scalar). Velocity = displacement/time (vector). Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. Instantaneous velocity is the velocity right now — the slope of the tangent on a position–time graph.

questions.q: Average velocity is defined as:
questions.explanation: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time. Using distance instead gives average speed.

questions.q: A runner covers 400 m east in 50 s. Find the average velocity.
questions.explanation: v = 400/50 = 8 m/s east

questions.q: A car can have a high average speed but a low average velocity.
questions.explanation: If the car winds around and returns near its start, distance is large (high speed) but displacement is small (low velocity).

questions.q: The speedometer in a car shows:
questions.explanation: A speedometer shows the speed at the current moment — instantaneous speed.

questions.q: On a position–time graph, what does the slope represent?
questions.explanation: The slope of a position–time graph is the velocity (rate of change of position).

questions.q: What is the SI unit of velocity?
questions.explanation: Velocity is measured in meters per second (m/s) in SI units.

g10-physics-up2-t3.overview: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. Whenever an object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction, it is accelerating. Understanding acceleration is key to explaining most real-world motion.
objectives: Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity
Calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time
Distinguish acceleration from velocity
Understand that slowing down is also acceleration (negative)
g10-physics-up2-t3.simple: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. If your car goes from 0 to 60 km/h in 6 seconds, it's accelerating. If it brakes from 60 to 0 in 3 seconds, it's ALSO accelerating — just in the negative direction (decelerating). Even turning a corner is acceleration because the direction of velocity changes!
g10-physics-up2-t3.detailed:
Acceleration (a) is the rate of change of velocity:

a = Δv / Δt = (v − u) / (t₂ − t₁)

where u is the initial velocity, v is the final velocity, and Δt is the time taken.

Acceleration is a vector — it has magnitude and direction. The SI unit is meters per second squared (m/s²).

Positive acceleration means velocity is increasing in the positive direction. Negative acceleration (deceleration) means velocity is decreasing or increasing in the negative direction.

Uniform acceleration means the velocity changes by the same amount each second — the acceleration is constant.

A common acceleration is free fall: g = 9.8 m/s² downward. This is the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface.

keyTerms.def: Rate of change of velocity (m/s²).
Negative acceleration — velocity decreasing.
Constant acceleration; velocity changes equally each second.
Motion under gravity alone, acceleration g = 9.8 m/s².
Velocity at the start of the time interval.
Velocity at the end of the time interval.

formulas.name: Acceleration
formulas.meaning: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken.
formulas.when: To find acceleration from initial and final velocity over a known time.

workedExamples.problem: A car accelerates from rest (u = 0) to 30 m/s in 6 seconds. Find its acceleration.
workedExamples.given: u = 0 m/s, v = 30 m/s, t = 6 s
workedExamples.answer: Acceleration = 5 m/s² (in the direction of motion)

workedExamples.problem: A train moving at 25 m/s comes to a stop in 10 s. Find its acceleration.
workedExamples.given: u = 25 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 10 s

commonMistakes: Thinking acceleration means 'speeding up' only. Slowing down and changing direction are also acceleration.
Forgetting units: m/s², not m/s.
Mixing up initial (u) and final (v) velocity in the formula.
Ignoring the sign of acceleration (direction).
applications: Car safety: airbags and crumple zones increase the time over which you decelerate, reducing the force (and injury).
Roller coasters: designers use acceleration limits to keep rides exciting but safe.
Space travel: rockets accelerate continuously, and astronauts feel this as G-forces.
g10-physics-up2-t3.summary: Acceleration = (v − u)/t, measured in m/s². It's the rate of change of velocity. Speeding up, slowing down, and turning all involve acceleration. Gravity provides a = 9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface.

questions.q: What is the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface?

g10-physics-up2-t4.overview: These four equations connect displacement, velocity, acceleration, and time for objects moving with constant acceleration. They are the workhorses of kinematics — master them and you can solve almost any motion problem.
objectives: State the four equations of motion
Identify the variables in each equation
Choose the right equation for a given problem
Solve problems involving constant acceleration step by step
g10-physics-up2-t4.simple: These equations are like a toolkit. Each one connects 4 of the 5 motion variables: u (start speed), v (end speed), a (acceleration), t (time), s (displacement). If you know any 3, you can find the 4th. It's like a recipe — pick the right equation, plug in the numbers, solve!
g10-physics-up2-t4.detailed:
For motion with constant acceleration, where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, and s = displacement:

1. v = u + at — relates final velocity to initial velocity, acceleration, and time.

2. s = ut + ½at² — displacement in terms of initial velocity, acceleration, and time.

3. v² = u² + 2as — useful when time is NOT known.

4. s = ½(u + v)t — displacement as the average velocity (½(u+v)) times time.

Solving strategy: Write down what's given. Identify what you need. Pick the equation containing all of them. Watch the signs: up/forward = positive, down/backward = negative. For objects in free fall, a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward.

keyTerms.def: Velocity at t = 0.
Velocity at the end of the time interval.
Change in position (vector).
Acceleration that doesn't change over time.
Motion under gravity only, a = g.

formulas.name: Equation 1 (velocity–time)
formulas.when: You know u, a, t and want v (or any rearrangement).

formulas.name: Equation 2 (displacement–time)
formulas.meaning: Displacement depends on the initial velocity term and the acceleration term.
formulas.when: You know u, a, t and want displacement.

formulas.name: Equation 3 (velocity–displacement)
formulas.meaning: Relates velocities and displacement without needing time.
formulas.when: Time is not given and you need to connect velocities and displacement.

formulas.name: Equation 4 (average velocity)
formulas.meaning: Displacement equals average velocity times time (for constant acceleration).
formulas.when: You know both velocities and time.

workedExamples.problem: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² for 8 seconds. Find (a) its final velocity and (b) the distance traveled.
workedExamples.given: u = 0 m/s, a = 3 m/s², t = 8 s
workedExamples.formula: (a) v = u + at; (b) s = ut + ½at²

workedExamples.problem: A ball is thrown downward with initial velocity 5 m/s from a height of 20 m. Find its velocity just before hitting the ground (a = g = 9.8 m/s²).
workedExamples.given: u = 5 m/s (downward), s = 20 m, a = 9.8 m/s²

commonMistakes: Using the wrong equation — write down what you know first, then choose.
Forgetting to square t in s = ut + ½at².
Sign errors: define up as positive and stick to it.
Using average speed formula when acceleration is not constant (the equations only work for constant acceleration!).
applications: Accident reconstruction: police use skid marks (distance) and friction to estimate a car's speed using v² = u² + 2as.
Engineering: elevator design uses these equations to ensure smooth, safe acceleration profiles.
Sports science: analyzing jump height from takeoff velocity.
g10-physics-up2-t4.summary: The four equations of motion (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = ½(u+v)t) apply ONLY to constant acceleration. Strategy: list givens → identify target → pick equation → solve with signs.

g10-physics-up2-t5.overview: Graphs turn motion into pictures you can read. Position–time, velocity–time, and acceleration–time graphs each tell a different story about how an object moves — and they're all connected.
objectives: Interpret position–time graphs (slope = velocity)
Interpret velocity–time graphs (slope = acceleration, area = displacement)
Sketch graphs for different types of motion
Convert between graph types
g10-physics-up2-t5.simple: A position–time graph shows where an object is at each moment — a straight line means constant velocity, a curve means acceleration. A velocity–time graph shows how fast it's going — the slope is acceleration and the area under the graph is the distance traveled. Reading graphs is like reading a story about the motion!
g10-physics-up2-t5.detailed:
Position–time (x–t) graphs:

  • The slope at any point = instantaneous velocity.
  • A straight line = constant velocity (uniform motion).
  • A steeper line = faster motion.
  • A curved line = changing velocity (acceleration). A parabola means constant acceleration.
  • A horizontal line = object at rest (position not changing).

Velocity–time (v–t) graphs:

  • The slope = acceleration.
  • The area under the graph = displacement.
  • A horizontal line = constant velocity (zero acceleration).
  • A sloped line = constant acceleration.

Acceleration–time (a–t) graphs:

  • A horizontal line at zero = constant velocity.
  • A horizontal line above zero = constant positive acceleration.
  • The area under the graph = change in velocity.

keyTerms.def: Rise over run on a graph; represents velocity on x–t, acceleration on v–t.
On v–t graphs, represents displacement.
A line touching a curve at one point; its slope gives instantaneous rate.
Where the graph crosses an axis.

formulas.name: Slope of a graph
formulas.meaning: The slope between two points is the vertical change divided by the horizontal change.
formulas.units: Depends on the axes (m/s for x–t graphs, m/s² for v–t graphs).
formulas.when: To find the rate of change represented by a straight-line graph.
formulas.example: On an x–t graph, a line rising 10 m over 2 s has slope 5 m/s = velocity.

workedExamples.problem: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (4 s, 8 m/s). Find (a) the acceleration and (b) the displacement.
workedExamples.given: Initial velocity 0, final velocity 8 m/s, time 4 s.
workedExamples.formula: (a) a = slope = Δv/Δt. (b) displacement = area under graph = ½ × base × height.
workedExamples.calculation: The graph forms a triangle of base 4 and height 8.

commonMistakes: Confusing the meanings: slope on x–t is velocity, on v–t is acceleration.
Forgetting that the AREA under a v–t graph is displacement (not the slope).
Reading curved graphs as straight lines — the slope of a curve changes continuously.
applications: Physicists and engineers read motion graphs to analyze everything from vehicle crash tests to particle accelerators.
Biomedical: gait analysis uses position/time graphs to study walking patterns.
Smartphone sensors produce acceleration–time graphs that apps interpret (step counters!).
g10-physics-up2-t5.summary: On x–t graphs: slope = velocity, curve = acceleration. On v–t graphs: slope = acceleration, area = displacement. On a–t graphs: area = change in velocity. Practice sketching and reading these graphs — they appear on every exam.

questions.explanation: The slope of an x–t graph is the rate of change of position = velocity.

questions.q: On a velocity–time graph, the area under the curve represents:
questions.explanation: Area under a v–t graph = velocity × time = displacement.

questions.q: On a velocity–time graph, the slope represents:
questions.explanation: Slope of v–t graph = change in velocity ÷ time = acceleration.

questions.explanation: A horizontal line on x–t means position isn't changing — the object is AT REST (velocity = 0).

questions.q: What shape does a position–time graph have for constant acceleration from rest?

g10-physics-up2-t6.overview: Motion is always relative to something. When you're on a train, the world outside seems to move backward. Relative velocity tells you how fast one object is moving as seen from another object.
objectives: Explain that velocity is measured relative to a reference frame
Calculate relative velocity for objects moving in the same direction
Calculate relative velocity for objects moving in opposite directions
Solve simple problems involving trains, cars, and rivers
g10-physics-up2-t6.simple: If you're driving at 80 km/h and a car passes you at 90 km/h, the other car is only going 10 km/h faster than you — that's the relative velocity. If two cars drive toward each other at 60 km/h each, they approach at 120 km/h! Velocity depends on who's watching.
g10-physics-up2-t6.detailed:
Relative velocity is the velocity of one object as observed from another object.

For two objects A and B moving along the same line:

Same direction: vAB = vA − vB

If A moves at 80 km/h and B at 60 km/h in the same direction, A's velocity relative to B is 80 − 60 = 20 km/h.

Opposite directions: vAB = vA − (−vB) = vA + vB

If A moves east at 60 km/h and B moves west at 60 km/h, they approach each other at 120 km/h.

The formula vAB = vA − vB works universally: the velocity of A relative to B is A's velocity minus B's velocity (treating directions with signs).

keyTerms.def: Velocity of one object measured from another moving object.
The coordinate system (observer) from which motion is measured.
The point of view from which motion is described.

formulas.name: Relative velocity (1D)
formulas.meaning: The velocity of A relative to B equals A's velocity minus B's velocity (with signs for direction).

vars.name: v_AB
vars.meaning: velocity of A relative to B

formulas.units: Same as the velocities (m/s or km/h).
formulas.when: To find how fast one moving object approaches or recedes from another.
formulas.example: A car at 90 km/h passes a truck at 70 km/h (same direction): relative velocity = 20 km/h.

workedExamples.problem: Two trains move on parallel tracks. Train A moves east at 30 m/s, Train B moves east at 20 m/s. What is the velocity of A relative to B?
workedExamples.given: v_A = 30 m/s east, v_B = 20 m/s east
workedExamples.answer: A moves 10 m/s east relative to B (A is pulling away).

workedExamples.problem: Car A moves east at 25 m/s. Car B moves west at 15 m/s. Find the velocity of A relative to B.
workedExamples.answer: A approaches B at 40 m/s east (they close at 40 m/s).

commonMistakes: Adding velocities when objects move the same direction (should subtract).
Forgetting signs for direction.
Thinking relative velocity only matters for trains — it applies to everything moving!
applications: Driving: judging overtaking speed needs relative velocity.
Aviation: mid-air collision avoidance is all about relative velocity.
River crossing: a boat's velocity relative to the bank combines its own velocity and the current.
g10-physics-up2-t6.summary: Relative velocity compares motion between two objects: v_AB = v_A − v_B. Same direction → subtract; opposite directions → add. The answer's sign shows direction.
